records.note: No unit conversion. The ' | ' in the row quotes is my cell separator for the HTML table; the cell values are verbatim. Values are means; the paper prints an uncertainty after each (e.g. 2.43±0.070). The swelling measure is a ratio of particle diameters (linear, not volume) between swollen (20 C) and collapsed (50 C) states of colloidal microgel particles, not the water uptake of a bulk gel. The paper prints no modulus-versus-crosslinker table; moduli appear only in figures.

candidate_laws.statement: In dense microgel suspensions the heating-versus-cooling asymmetry of the storage modulus recovery (Kovacs asymmetry) is non-monotonic in particle stiffness and peaks at intermediate crosslinker content; the values are shown only in figures.
candidate_laws.quote: Our data revealed a pronounced, non-monotonic asymmetry in G′ with increasing particle stiffness, with maximum asymmetry observed in intermediate-stiffness particle suspensions.

papers.why: It is about hovering insect wings, which have no forward cruising speed, so our swimmer Strouhal law does not apply; it proposes a different vortex-formation Strouhal number that sits near 0.15 to 0.17.

candidate_laws.statement: A vortex-formation Strouhal number built from twice the wingbeat frequency, a separated-flow length and a separation velocity falls in about 0.15 to 0.17 for hovering insects, the same range as bluff-body vortex shedding. The body text gives the insect mean as 0.162 with spread 0.038 and the stationary-wing value as 0.171 with spread 0.018 (the plus-minus sign was lost in the PDF text layer, so those are not quoted here).
candidate_laws.quote: identifies a universal vortex-formation Strouhal-number range of approximately 0.15 to 0.17. Here we show that this same range governs LEV formation on both stationary wings and hovering insect wings.

papers.title: A Universal Vortex-Formation Law for Insect Hovering
